paras: The threatened lynching of John Wesley took place in St. Louis County, Missouri, in late August and early September 1895, when armed citizens' posses hunted Wesley, a Black man accused of attempting to assault an aged widow at Manchester, intending to hang him. Deputy sheriffs captured him early on September 4 and lodged him in the county jail at Clayton, where the last reports leave him. Wire dispatches carried the manhunt nationally, often under headlines forecasting a hanging.

According to the first wire, Wesley had just completed a five-year term in the penitentiary for an attempted criminal assault, which some versions said was upon a girl. A special to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch added that he had made himself "notorious" by repeated unsuccessful attempts to assault Miss Ellen Tumilty, who lived about three miles from Manchester.

Wesley was accused of attempting to assault a widow on the outskirts of Manchester about 11 o'clock on Friday night, August 30. Most reports named her Mrs. Rosalie Marmion, and the Record-Union gave her age as 77, but the Post-Dispatch special called her Mrs. Rosalie Newman. By midnight a posse "with a rope" was searching for him, and the Manchester wire said that if captured "he will be strung up."

The constable organized a separate party which, a Manchester dispatch said, meant to capture Wesley and "if possible, save him from being lynched." By September 1 a sheriff's posse of ten deputies and 25 citizens "intent on lynching Wesley" were searching the woods of the northern county, and the Record-Union wrote that his only chance for life was capture by the sheriff's men. A report from Gumbo that he had been taken proved untrue. On September 3 a St. Louis dispatch described two posses of over 100 men each, one under Constable Schumaker, and said that if the citizens' posse caught him he would "certainly be hanged at once."

At 1 o'clock on the morning of September 4, Wesley forced his way into the kitchen of Colonel Williams near Baldwin, where Deputy Sheriffs Hancken and George were asleep, and the two deputies overpowered him. He was driven by carriage to the county jail at Clayton and placed in a steel cell at 3 o'clock that morning. The Potosi Journal, a Missouri paper, said he had been arrested while breaking into a house at Ballwin "to get something to eat."

According to the officers' account carried in the capture dispatches, Wesley made a full confession. The same dispatch described feeling in the vicinity as "intense" but said no attempt at lynching was expected. No report of an indictment, trial or sentence was found.

White papers ran short wire items under headlines anticipating a hanging: "Prospective Lynching" (Santa Fe Daily New Mexican), "Will Be Hung if Caught" (Evening Times) and "Sure to Swing" (Birmingham Age-Herald). Weeklies in Kansas and Nebraska ran "If Caught He Will Swing From a Tree" and "Two Bands Near St. Louis Determined to Lynch a Negro Wretch," and texts throughout called Wesley a "brute."

Rumor sometimes ran ahead of fact: the Salt Lake Herald added a bulletin that mobs had "captured and lynched Wesley at Gumbo," noting that confirmation was lacking. After the capture, the Rock Island Argus headed its brief "Has Been Duly Lynched by this Time" over a text reporting that Wesley was in jail. Capture briefs called him "the Manchester, Mo., rapist," and the Savannah Morning News headed its story "Rapist in a Cell," though the first dispatches described an unsuccessful attempt.

A widely reprinted dispatch said "half the farmers of St. Louis county" had hunted him intending to hang him or burn him "alive at a stake." All the reports located were in white papers, from August 31 to September 12; no Black newspaper account was found.

The widow appears as Newman in the Post-Dispatch special and as Marmion, Marmon, Marimon or Marion elsewhere, Marmion being most common. Early dispatches and the capture report described an attempted assault, while later St. Louis dispatches said Wesley "assaulted" her after a "desperate struggle." The Potosi Journal put the arrest "a week later" at Ballwin; the capture dispatches place it five days after the alleged attempt, near Baldwin.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of John Wesley
bases: Armed citizens' posses hunted John Wesley with a rope and declared they would hang him, but deputy sheriffs captured and jailed him first, so the episode is a threatened lynching (A2, A7, A13).

A citizens' party of 25, later reported at over 100, searched for Wesley in order to hang him for an alleged attempted assault, without lawful authority (A7, A9); he was captured by deputies and jailed alive, and no killing was confirmed (A8, A13, A22).

The Post-Dispatch special, the Manchester wire, later St. Louis dispatches and a Missouri weekly agree on the manhunt and the capture (A1, A2, A13, A22); a single unconfirmed bulletin of a lynching at Gumbo was denied the next day (A5, A8).

accounts.label: Post-Dispatch special from Manchester
accounts.gist: A 'fiendish' attempt on Mrs. Rosalie Newman by Wesley, notorious for attempts on Ellen Tumilty; the people organized a posse and there would 'surely' be a lynching if they caught him before the officers.

accounts.label: Manchester wire, Aug. 31
accounts.gist: Wesley, just out of the penitentiary, made an unsuccessful attempt on the aged widow Mrs. Rosalie Marmion; a posse with a rope searched from midnight and would string him up.

accounts.label: Unconfirmed bulletin
accounts.gist: A 2:10 a.m. bulletin said mobs from Manchester and Baldwin had captured and lynched Wesley at Gumbo; it noted confirmation was lacking, and a St. Louis dispatch the next day called the Gumbo capture report untrue.

accounts.label: St. Louis dispatches, Sept. 1-3
accounts.gist: Sheriff's and citizens' posses searched the woods; the citizens' party meant to lynch him and he would be hanged at once if they caught him.

accounts.label: Capture report (officers' account)
accounts.gist: Deputies sleeping at Colonel Williams's overpowered Wesley when he forced his way into the kitchen, drove him to the Clayton jail, and reported a full confession; no lynching attempt was expected.

accounts.label: Missouri state news column
accounts.gist: Wesley was arrested a week after the assault while breaking into a house at Ballwin to get something to eat.

framing.detail: The Post-Dispatch special, headed 'Prospective Lynching' and 'Fiendish Effort to Outrage a Respected Widow', forecast a hanging without disapproval.
Short wire items ran under 'Will Be Hung if Caught', 'Sure to Swing' and 'A Posse With a Rope', repeating that he would be 'strung up'.
Kansas and Nebraska weeklies stacked headlines such as 'Sure Death', 'If Caught He Will Swing From a Tree' and 'Two Bands Near St. Louis Determined to Lynch a Negro Wretch'.
The capture dispatch reported the arrest and confession in plain terms and said no lynching attempt was expected.
Capture briefs called him 'the Manchester, Mo., rapist' and 'Rapist in a Cell', and the Rock Island Argus headed its brief 'Has Been Duly Lynched by this Time' over a jail report.
